newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope receives Iran envoy, urges respect for law.
newsitem.headline: Pope receives Iran envoy, urges respect for law.

text.p: Pope John Paul called for respect for international law and a commitment to ease global tensions on Saturday when he received Iran's new ambassador to the Vatican.

"Only in a world of justice and peace can people live in obedience to God and in the generous service of their fellow humans," the Pope told Mohammad Hadi Abd Khodai, who presented his diplomatic credentials.

"Respect for international law and commitment to negotiations as a way to ease global tension are imperative means to building a better world where well-being and religion can flourish," the 76-year-old Pontiff said.
About 12,000 Roman Catholics live in Iran, one of the world's most militantly Islamic countries.
"The Holy See counts on the Iranian authorities to ensure that they will continue to worship in freedom," said the Pope, who is set to travel to Lebanon later this month.
No Pope in modern times has gone to Lebanon, where Israel accuses Iran of actively arming the Hizbollah Shi'ite Moslem guerrilla group.
The Pope, who often calls for Middle East peace and dreams of visiting the Holy Land by the year 2000, is expected to urge a comprehensive settlement in the region during his trip.
The Vatican's position on Iran contrasts with that of the United States, which blasted the Holy See last March when it established diplomatic ties with Libya.
The U.S. has urged the international community to isolate both countries, saying they are sponsors of terrorism.

The Vatican has said it had hoped its ties with Libya would give a "particular impulse" to international dialogue and underscore its view that the Mediterranean should be "a region of peace, stability and security".
It also said ties with Tripoli were forged partly to tend to the 50,000 Catholics who live in the North African nation.
